iCan.en: I can use German nominative personal pronouns (ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie) as sentence subjects.
I can conjugate sein and haben in the present tense to describe people, states, and possessions.
I can conjugate regular German verbs in the present tense.
I can conjugate common stem-changing verbs like sprechen, lesen, fahren, and schlafen in the present tense.
I can build German statements with the conjugated verb in second position, including inversion after time or place.
I can ask and answer W-questions using wer, was, wo, woher, wohin, wann, and wie.
I can form yes/no questions by placing the conjugated verb in first position and answer with ja, nein, or doch.
I can use definite (der, die, das) and indefinite (ein, eine) articles with masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns.
I can form common German noun plurals and use them with the plural article die.
I can negate nouns with kein/keine and verbs, adjectives, or sentences with nicht.
I can use definite, indefinite, and negative articles in the accusative case for direct objects.
I can use accusative personal pronouns (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie) as direct objects.
I can use possessive determiners (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr) in the nominative and accusative.
I can use modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, möchten) with an infinitive at the end of the clause.
I can use separable verbs like aufstehen, einkaufen, and anrufen with the prefix at the end of a main clause.
I can give instructions, advice, and polite requests using the imperative for du, ihr, and Sie.

name.en: Past tense of sein and haben

iCan.en: I can talk about past states and possessions using the simple past forms of sein (war) and haben (hatte).
I can talk about past actions using the Perfekt with haben and regular or common irregular past participles.
I can form the Perfekt with sein for verbs of movement and change of state like gehen, fahren, and bleiben.
I can form the Partizip II of separable verbs (eingekauft), inseparable verbs (verstanden), and -ieren verbs (studiert).
I can say where people and places are or where I am going using in, aus, nach, zu, and bei.
I can give times, days, and seasons using um, am, im, and von … bis.
I can connect main clauses with und, oder, aber, denn, and sondern without changing word order.
I can use definite, indefinite, and negative articles in the dative case (dem, der, dem, den + -n).
I can use dative personal pronouns (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen) in everyday sentences.
I can use common dative verbs such as helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken, schmecken, and passen.
I can build sentences with both a dative and an accusative object in the right order (e.g. Ich gebe dir das Buch).
I can choose between dative (Wo?) and accusative (Wohin?) after an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, and zwischen.
I can use prepositions that always take the accusative case (für, durch, gegen, ohne, um, bis).
I can use prepositions that always take the dative case (aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber).
I can use possessive determiners (meinem, deiner, ihren, etc.) in the dative case.
I can use common reflexive verbs like sich freuen, sich treffen, and sich die Hände waschen.
I can talk about past abilities, duties, and plans using konnte, musste, wollte, durfte, and sollte.
I can form subordinate clauses with weil and dass, placing the conjugated verb at the end.
I can express conditions and time relationships using wenn (present, future, repeated past) and als (single past event).
I can ask polite indirect questions using ob and question words with the verb at the end.
I can add the right adjective endings (-e or -en) after definite articles like der, die, das, and dieser.
I can add the right adjective endings after ein, kein, and possessive determiners in nominative, accusative, and dative.
I can compare people and things using the comparative, superlative (am …-sten), so … wie, and als.
I can make polite requests, suggestions, and wishes using könnte, hätte, wäre, sollte, and würde + infinitive.
I can use common verb-preposition combinations like warten auf, denken an, and sich interessieren für with the right case.
I can ask about and refer back to things with prepositions using worauf, womit, darauf, and darüber.
I can use dieser, welcher, jeder, man, jemand, niemand, etwas, and nichts accurately in context.
I can link ideas with deshalb, trotzdem, danach, zuerst, and dann using verb-second inversion.
I can conjugate werden to describe changes (es wird kalt) and prepare for future and passive structures.
I can understand and use the Präteritum of regular and common irregular verbs in written reports and stories.
I can express that one past event happened before another using the Plusquamperfekt with hatte or war.
I can express plans, promises, forecasts, and assumptions using Futur I (werden + infinitive).
I can describe processes and actions without naming the actor using the present passive (werden + Partizip II).
I can form the past passive (wurde + Partizip II) and passive sentences with modal verbs (kann/muss … werden).
I can use the genitive case (des, der, eines, einer) for possession and after wegen, trotz, während, and statt.
I can use strong adjective endings without an article (e.g. frisches Brot, mit kaltem Wasser, gute Freunde).
I can describe people and things more precisely using relative clauses in nominative, accusative, and dative.
I can form relative clauses with prepositions (auf den, mit der) and genitive relative pronouns (dessen, deren).
I can use infinitive clauses with zu, um … zu, ohne … zu, and (an)statt … zu.
I can connect ideas with obwohl, während, bevor, nachdem, seit(dem), and bis in subordinate clauses.
I can express purpose with damit (different subjects) and results with sodass.
I can structure arguments using sowohl … als auch, weder … noch, nicht nur … sondern auch, zwar … aber, and je … desto.
I can express hypothetical situations and unreal wishes using wenn-clauses with Konjunktiv II.
I can express past regrets and unrealized past possibilities using hätte or wäre + Partizip II.
I can use present participles (ein lachendes Kind) and past participles (ein gelesenes Buch) as declined adjectives.
I can decline common weak masculine nouns like der Mensch, der Kollege, and der Student with -n/-en outside the nominative singular.
I can order time, cause, manner, and place adverbials naturally inside the German sentence bracket.
I can recognize and use common modal particles (doch, mal, ja, eben, halt) to add tone in spoken German.
I can greet people, say goodbye, and give basic personal details like my name, age, and country.
I can understand and say numbers, prices in euros and cents, and phone numbers.
I can tell the time (formal and informal) and name days of the week, months, and dates.
I can name family members, friends, and basic marital/relationship words.
I can name classroom objects and school subjects and use basic classroom phrases.
I can name everyday foods, drinks, meals, and shops and ask for items and prices.
I can name rooms, furniture, and everyday household items to describe a home.
I can describe my daily routine, hobbies, and favorite free-time activities.
I can name basic parts of the body and say when something hurts or I feel sick.
I can name places in town and means of transport and understand simple directions.
I can name colors, seasons, and basic weather conditions.
I can describe clothes, sizes, physical appearance, and basic personality traits.
I can use vocabulary for booking trips, tickets, hotels, luggage, and holiday activities.
I can name common professions, workplaces, and everyday work activities.
I can describe symptoms, understand simple advice at the doctor's or pharmacy, and talk about staying healthy.
I can invite someone, accept or decline invitations, and express good wishes for birthdays and holidays.
I can talk about using smartphones, computers, emails, apps, and television.
I can express feelings, preferences, agreement, and disagreement in everyday situations.
I can name landscapes, animals, plants, and simple ways to protect the environment.
I can handle everyday errands at the post office, bank, library, or lost-and-found office.
I can understand and form everyday German compound nouns and determine their article from the final noun.
I can use vocabulary for school qualifications, apprenticeships, CVs, and job interviews.
I can discuss environmental problems, climate protection, recycling, and sustainable habits.
I can talk about rules, rights, volunteering, and living together in a diverse society.
I can discuss news reports, social media, privacy, and advertising using B1 media vocabulary.
I can talk about films, concerts, books, exhibitions, and cultural events.
I can discuss spending habits, online shopping, warranties, and product complaints.
I can talk about balanced nutrition, exercise, stress, and healthcare.
I can use B1 phrases to state opinions, weigh pros and cons, give examples, and propose compromises.
I can deduce and form words using common prefixes and suffixes such as un-, -ung, -heit/-keit, -lich, and -bar.
I can pronounce the German alphabet and spell out names and words clearly.
I can pronounce and spell German umlauts (ä, ö, ü) and diphthongs (ei, eu/äu, au) accurately.

name.en: Key consonant sounds (ch, sch, sp, st)

iCan.en: I can pronounce the ich- and ach-sounds (ch), sch, initial sp/st, and z/tz reliably.
I can hear, pronounce, and recognize spelling cues for long vowels (ie, silent h) and short vowels (double consonants).
I can capitalize sentence beginnings, all German nouns, and the formal pronoun Sie.
I can stress the main syllable of German words and use falling or rising intonation in statements and questions.
I can pronounce final b, d, g as p, t, k (e.g. Tag, Kind, gelb) and still spell them correctly.
I can pronounce German r-sounds and reduced unstressed endings (-er, -en, -el) naturally.
I can stress separable verb prefixes (aufstehen, einkaufen) and leave inseparable prefixes (verstehen, beginnen) unstressed.
I can decide whether to write s, ss, or ß based on vowel length and voicing.
I can place commas in lists and before subordinate clauses introduced by weil, dass, wenn, or als.
I can shift sentence stress to highlight new information or express contrast in conversation.
I can pronounce and stress common international loanwords in German (e.g. -tion, -ie, -ieren, -tät).
I can set commas accurately around relative clauses and infinitive clauses with um/ohne/statt … zu.
I can write German compounds as single words and capitalize nominalized verbs and adjectives (das Lesen, alles Gute).
I can choose appropriately between informal du and formal Sie when addressing people in German-speaking countries.
I can locate Germany, Austria, and Switzerland and name their capitals and major cities.
I can use typical greeting, thanking, and apologizing conventions in German-speaking everyday life.
I can describe typical meal times, bakeries, cafés, and restaurant customs (such as tipping and paying) in D-A-CH.
I can compare a typical school day and school holidays in German-speaking countries with my own.
I can name major public holidays and seasonal traditions in German-speaking countries (e.g. Weihnachten, Ostern, Silvester).
I can navigate trains, S-Bahn, U-Bahn, buses, timetables, and ticket validation in D-A-CH.
I can explain everyday housing norms in D-A-CH such as Hausordnung, quiet hours, and waste separation.
I can describe regional customs and festivals across Germany, Austria, and Switzerland (e.g. Karneval, Oktoberfest, Nationalfeiertage).
I can explain the role of sports and leisure clubs (Vereine) and free-time culture in D-A-CH.
I can describe the main school tracks and vocational training (Ausbildung) in German-speaking countries.
I can recognize common Austrian and Swiss German everyday words (e.g. Grüezi, Servus, Jänner, Velo, Paradeiser).
I can explain key workplace norms in German-speaking countries such as punctuality, direct feedback, and application customs.
I can name major German-language news outlets and public broadcasters and compare media habits.
I can explain everyday sustainability practices in D-A-CH such as bottle deposits (Pfand), recycling, and green mobility.
I can outline key milestones of post-war German history, the fall of the Berlin Wall, and European integration.
I can compare cultural norms, question stereotypes, and handle misunderstandings politely in intercultural encounters.
I can distinguish standard German, regional varieties (D-A-CH), colloquial speech, and formal register.
I can understand and fill in simple registration or hotel forms with my personal details.
I can extract key facts from short signs, opening hours, timetables, and public notices.
I can understand short text messages, postcards, and simple personal notes.
I can write short messages, postcards, or simple emails to invite someone or ask for basic information.
I can pick out key details like times, prices, and platform numbers from short announcements and voicemails.
I can manage short everyday dialogues such as ordering food, shopping, and asking simple questions.
I can introduce myself in a few simple connected sentences about my name, home, family, and hobbies.
I can pass on simple key facts (times, places, prices) from a short notice or message in another language.
I can read and write informal emails and personal messages about everyday plans, news, and invitations.
I can scan advertisements, flyers, menus, and event schedules to find specific details.
I can understand the main points of short, simple articles and blog posts on familiar everyday topics.
I can tell or write a short account of a weekend, trip, or past event in chronological order.
I can make, change, or cancel appointments and plan an activity together with someone.
I can understand the main points and details of clear everyday conversations and short radio clips.
I can describe people, places, and activities shown in a picture using simple connected sentences.
I can summarize useful information from flyers, emails, or schedules for someone in another language.
I can write semi-formal and formal emails or letters for inquiries, apologies, complaints, and applications.
I can understand main ideas, structure, and key details in newspaper articles and factual texts on familiar topics.
I can read and write structured opinion posts in forums or blogs, giving reasons and personal examples.
I can prepare and deliver a short, structured presentation on a familiar topic with introduction, pros/cons, and conclusion.
I can take part in discussions on familiar topics, explain my point of view, and react to others' arguments.
I can follow interviews, radio discussions, news items, and short videos on familiar topics in standard German.
I can understand the plot, characters, and main message of simple German short stories and song lyrics.
I can summarize the main points and opinions of a German article or discussion for someone in another language.
